title: Synthetic AI contact can lower the short-run barrier to cross-partisan engagement
source_unit: Five preregistered experiments with online U.S. partisan participants; study-specific participant, within-person, and behavioral-choice units are preserved

mortality_reflection_equivalent_ai.unit: minutes accepted as equally aversive to a three-minute AI outgroup conversation

mortality_reflection_equivalent_human.unit: minutes accepted as equally aversive to a three-minute live-human outgroup conversation

observations.method: Between-subjects randomized comparison of an AI outgroup partner and a live human outgroup partner, with an incentive-compatible mortality-reflection alternative.
observations.uncertainty: This measures aversion to the experimental conversation, not ordinary political contact, general AI preference, or durable openness. The online sample and mortality-reflection task limit generalization.
observations.subgroup: Democrats and Republicans; the paper reports the comparison held across parties and extremity range.
observations.counterinterpretation: Participants may find an AI interaction less socially threatening without becoming more receptive to real people or opposing ideas outside the experiment.

denominator.unit: U.S. partisan participants measured before and after a ten-minute outgroup-bot conversation

outgroup_warmth_change.unit: points on a 0-100 outgroup warmth thermometer

observations.method: Within-person pre/post design in which participants conversed with a chatbot prompted to represent their political outgroup and then re-rated warmth and beliefs.
observations.uncertainty: Pre/post movement is not equivalent to a fully controlled between-person effect. It does not establish persistence, policy agreement, institutional trust, or real-world action.
observations.subgroup: Democrats and Republicans; topic was environmental-consumption attitudes.
observations.counterinterpretation: Repeated measurement, demand effects, novelty, or the structured research setting may contribute to immediate movement.

observations.method: Between-subjects randomized three-arm comparison of an outgroup-representing bot, an apolitical cats-versus-dogs chat, and Space Invaders.
observations.uncertainty: The study's main sample is Democrats and the measured outcome is warmth after one conversation. It does not show broad depolarization or prove that the bot's representation was accurate.
observations.subgroup: Democrats in the reported main design.
observations.counterinterpretation: The outgroup prompt, topic, or perceived informativeness may be unusually effective and may not generalize across parties, issues, or model versions.

observations.method: Between-subjects randomized five-minute outgroup-bot versus apolitical-chat experiment followed by an incentive-compatible choice between a real three-minute outgroup conversation and mortality reflection.
observations.uncertainty: The choice is immediate and experimentally structured. It is closer to action than an attitude item but does not establish later conversation quality, cooperation, voting, turnout, or policy agreement.
observations.subgroup: Democrats and Republicans; the paper reports a significant Republican shift and no significant treatment-by-party interaction.
observations.counterinterpretation: A willingness to choose one short conversation may reflect curiosity or novelty and may not translate into sustained cross-partisan relationships.

denominator.unit: U.S. Democratic participants assigned to outgroup-bot or apolitical-chat conditions

one_week_cohens_d.unit: Cohen's d in preregistered mean model; not statistically significant

observations.method: Between-subjects randomized outgroup-bot versus apolitical-chat experiment with immediate and one-week warmth measures.
observations.uncertainty: The one-week mean result is imprecise and the paper also reports an exploratory pooled residual. Neither establishes durable cultural change. Attrition, floor-bunching, and model specification remain relevant.
observations.subgroup: Democrats in the main study; the paper discusses persistence concentrated among more extreme participants in pooled follow-up work.
observations.counterinterpretation: A short intervention may need repetition or real social reinforcement; rapid decay may indicate that the immediate response was situational rather than a changed identity or belief.

related_sources.claim: The authors publish de-identified data and code that reproduce the released analyses; archive SHA-256 is preserved in the source record.
SSRN provides the provisional working-paper record, authorship, posting date, and abstract.

boundary: This record contains study-specific randomized evidence for aversion, warmth, belief accuracy, a costly immediate contact choice, and one-week persistence in online U.S. partisan samples. It does not establish durable depolarization, real-world cooperation, electoral behavior, institutional trust, population-scale cultural change, or safe governance. Preprint and replication-package status remain explicit.
